utterances.text: Now you can't mark on this one because it is a freeze-frame from a video. So the white building on the right with the arched windows, that is the museum, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: The more -- the more modern building on the left side with the square windows is the Faculty of Philosophy of the University, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And looking down that street, the trees are leafed out; but up above the leaves, you can see the top storey of - different people call it different things - the bank building or the Metalka building, can't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we don't know the number of this photograph. It hasn't been marked yet so that we can perhaps use it, if necessary, later on. We might need it later on, so it should be marked as a Prosecution Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is a new photograph, Mr. Docherty?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: No. It's not a new photograph, Your Honour. It's not a photograph. We have frozen a video frame on screen, like using the stop or a pause button on a DVD player. This is the 360-degree video from scheduled sniping incident 13. We can certainly put it back up, just as quickly as we did now, if the Defence wants to use it. I don't have the number on my -- we need to consult a list and find the number, but we can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, we are, or I am, having some concerns because I think it's a bit unfair to the Defence to show a 360-degree video from exactly this point, because obviously the red building would be behind the Faculty of Philosophy here. So there would be no direct line of sight from this point. But perhaps if we were to move westwards, there might be a chance that you perhaps could see the red building if you move over towards the museum. And my recollection is, but I may be wrong, but didn't we have a 360-degree video taken with Mrs. Sokolovic, exactly from the corner of the museum? Do you understand my point?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I understand your point. Give us a minute and we'll look. It takes us a minute, but no more than that. We'll have to take this off in order to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: We have the one you're looking for, Judge Harhoff. Would you like to see it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well, my proposition is that this might be more illustrative to what is the issue here, whether or not there is a direct line of sight from the red building to this crossing area, to the Marindvor area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let us see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Katic, this is a photograph that is taken on the sidewalk in front of the museum; and across the road, is that the Faculty of Philosophy of the University?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, we can move this left or right, as you wish, just let us know. But where is -- the red building is not visibly, is it, Mr. Katic.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't see any building, apart from the Faculty of Philosophy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am not against it at all. It would be great if we could keep this photograph for later, but we don't have a number for it. So how can we refer to it? How can we use it in our re-examination if we don't have a number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, he's right. Is there a number for this?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: There is a number. We're calling these up as the Chamber asks. There is a list, and we can consult it and get the number very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So we'll get the number, Mr. Tapuskovic, perhaps not right now, but we'll get it. It's a technical matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: The 65 ter number, Your Honour, is 02716. That's for the whole video, and any particular incident can be called up within that 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Katic, but there was a lot going on. I didn't hear your last -- last answer, which was: "I don't see any building, apart from the Faculty of Philosophy." Would you like us to move the photograph in either direction? This is a 360, so if I say to move it, you'll start to see the scenery rotate.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, right now, I can't see any other building, just the building of the Faculty of Philosophy.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Well, tell you what? Let's rotate the photograph; and if you see the red building, just let us know.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see any building in the territory held by the Republika Srpska army on this footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Could we look then at the one I wanted to show in the first place, which is number 13. Actually, it is one that is 13, but a little bit to the right. So let's do number 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, again, Mr. Katic, we'll rotate it; and if you see the red building, let us know.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stop. I can see the building now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: What building do you see?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the basis of this photograph, I cannot see whether this is building D [as interpreted] or the Invest building -- Invest Bank building. Building B or the bank, but it is not quite clear. Actually, you have to go a little bit further to the left in order to see it probably better.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Can we rotate it little bit to the left. Stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Does that help? I believe your testimony was that the building you saw was either the B building or the bank building; but in any event, not the red building; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And that's because there's tall buildings obstructing the line of sight from the red building to the S-curve area in front of the Holiday Inn; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You can't shoot the S-curve area from the red building, can you, Mr. Katic, because have you to shoot through the buildings in front of you to do so, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty, I'm not a very technical person. Doesn't it depend on where the photograph is taken from?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it doesn't, and that's why I'm a bit sorry we went down there path; although, I notice it was of my choosing. But I thought the photograph, as I said to Judge Harhoff, that was originally on there that the witness had marked showed pretty clearly that there were a number of tall buildings between the red building an and the Marindvor area. Judge Harhoff then said that it depended on elevations, and so we went with this. And witness has now testified, I believe, that you can see the D or the bank building - he's not sure which - but you can't see the red building. That's the only point I'm trying to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Katic, in your evidence in-chief, you testified about some events that occurred at the beginning of the armed conflict; and, in particular, I want to talk about the issue of people crossing -- civilians crossing -- I don't believe the witness is getting a translation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let that be attended to. We understand that you're not getting any translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Are you hearing me now in Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You testified on your evidence in-chief about some events which occurred in 1992, before the outbreak of the armed conflict. I want to go back to talked about question of people crossing, civilians, I should say, crossing from one side of the line to the other. First of all, it is true, Mr. Katic, is it not, that the area of Grbavica was ethnically cleansed by the Serbian authorities in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Could we please see 65 ter number 03188.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Katic, this is a letter from an official of the United Nations, Major-General Morillon, dated October 1st of 1992 and addressed to Radovan Karadzic. Have you seen this before, or do you need a minute to read it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen it before, but I do want to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Okay. I want to direct your attention, sir, to the bottom of the first paragraph. There's a reference there to the forced expulsion of nearly 300 persons from Grbavica. Do you see where I am reading?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Those 300 persons were not Serb persons, were they, Mr. Katic, and that's why this letter is being addressed to Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: These 300 persons were non-Serbs who were expelled from Grbavica by the Serbian authorities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I want to show you another document concerning this incident from October of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty, in the third paragraph, General Morillon says, "I'm willing to believe that you are not libel in this case."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: That's why I want to go to the next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Before I do that, I want to tender this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P755, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Then I'd like to have displayed on the screen 65 ter -- I'm sorry, 65 ter 3190 [Realtime transcript read in error "31890"].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid there might be a mistake about the number. Because as we marked it, it's 3190. I suppose that's the number that we noted down when we were marking this document. I don't know if it is correct. Without this 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is that so, Mr. Docherty?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not sure what 8 is being referred to, but this is 65 ter 3190, and that's the document I was looking for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let us proceed on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, this is an United Nations report prepared by a Colonel Theriault, and it is dated the 30th of September, 1992, the day before General Morillon's letter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And that indicates that United Nations officials were asked to go to the Bristol Hotel, in response to reports of an incompetence occurring there, and it states in the second paragraph that they confirmed that the expulsion was in progress and Muslims were gathering at the Bristol Hotel; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what's written.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And in the last paragraph on that page, about in the middle, it talks about "the sounds of shelling and gun-fire could be heard from inside. People were literally under panic." Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Okay. It's a sentence that begins: "Sounds of shelling and gun-fire ..."

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see this in my passage. I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be of assistance, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Katic, if you turn to page 2, on the B/C/S version, I believe it's line 4. We would have to show page 2 in B/C/S, line 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Then could we please at the bottom of the English in any event - and I don't know if there be on yet another page in the B/C/S - it indicates that "writer was able to confirm that approximately 300 Muslim civilians have been expelled by the Serbs during the day from the area of Grbavica. 150 of them gathered at the Bristol Hotel and the remaining at the assembly -- the BiH assembly building one kilometre to the east." Does it also say that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And could we go to the next page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Just one moment. I don't know if -- I think we'll need to go to the next page in B/C/S as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And this concerns shelling of these civilians gathered at the Bristol Hotel. In English, it says: "Based on the information," plus sign, "observations, it appeared evident that the shelling was directed towards the Muslim civilians. All of them were confined in a specific area, and the Serbians were well aware of that." Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether the Serbs were aware that those people were locked in one area. I told you where I was in 1992. And the previous passage and the one framed now referred to events in September and October 1992. As I have said before, it was in 1992 and, obviously, President Karadzic received this letter, and the authorities in Novo Sarajevo municipality were replaced. I said that on Thursday and Friday, and this evidence you are presenting, Prosecutor, probably was what caused this replacement of authorities. If you ask me about ethnic cleansing in Grbavica, I told you it didn't happen, because throughout the war, from the time when I became president in Grbavica, around 1500 non-Muslims -- non-Serbs lived in Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: But the question I was putting to you, Mr. Katic, was simply whether this document -- you have seen the document, and you continue to maintain that there was no cleansing in Grbavica. What word would you use to describe the events set out in General Morillon's letter and in this United Nations report?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You told me that Grbavica was ethnically cleansed. When you put it that way, that would mean that all non-Serbs were expelled. I said that was not true, because during the war 1500 non-Serbs lived in Grbavica. These problems occurred in 1992 and there were expulsions, and that is why the local authorities, the local government in the area of the Serbian municipality of Novo Sarajevo were replaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: So is it your testimony that as long as the expulsion does not result in the complete removal of all non-Serbs, you will not characterise it as ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot talk about expulsions in 1992, despite the fact that I read these documents. I know that the thing happened on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Katic, you answered a question that's a little bit different than the one I asked you. The one I asked you was -- I'm trying to get some clarification of your use of the verb "ethnic cleansing." Is it your testimony that as long as that does not result in the complete expulsion of all non-Serbs, you will decline to put the label "ethnic cleansing" on the action. Is that your testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my testimony that from the moment I took over the post of president, there was no ethnic cleansing on Grbavica and there was no expulsion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: But the distinction is still important, because I hear you saying that as long as some non-Serbs are left, this is not ethnic cleansing; and then you are saying there was no ethnic cleansing, which leaves open the question of what there was. Do you see where the confusion is coming from?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of these two papers referring to events in 1992, we could say that non-Serb population was expelled; but if I'm telling you that until the end of the war there were no more persecutions or expulsions or ethnic cleanses, you have to believe me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Well, let's -- first of all, you left the army on the 13th of March, 1993, because you had been elected president of the assembly of Srpsko Novo Sarajevo, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm just trying to get the chronology straight. And before that, although not president of the assembly, you had been, you had been a deputy, is that correct, but you had been able to as a deputy, even while serving in the army, because that was not so demanding a post as being president of the assembly; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: How long had you been a deputy before you came president of the assembly?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From October or maybe November 1990, until the day when I became president of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: So during the time that is referred to in these documents, you had been a member of the assembly. You had not been president of the assembly, I understand that, but you were a member of the assembly. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I tender this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P756, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And the next document I would like to show the witness is 65 ter number 01382. Could we just double-check this is 01382? Okay. Oh, I apologise. I read it wrong. 03182.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This one is not the right one either.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: No. This is the document I want, Mr. Katic. Mr. Katic, this document, I'll just read off the title and the date: "Instructions for the organisation and operation of organs of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina in emergency conditions, Sarajevo, 19 December 1991." Have I read that correctly.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I believe this document was circulated at different times under different dates. Have you seen this document before but with a different date?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Do you know a magazine called "Slobodna Bosna"?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard of it. I know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Are you aware that this document was reprinted in Slobodna Bosna, the text of this document, that is.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Could we look at paragraph number 4 in both English and B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I suggest that while we sort this out, it's a good time for a break, so we don't consume court time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it is time for the break. We'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Katic, while we were in the break, we sorted out the problem we were having with the document. On the screen in front of you, on the right-hand side, there is a block of this document. And I'm going to read, starting up at the top, and excuse me, it look like --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, the B/C/S page we had before the Court came in is no longer the B/C/S page. There we are. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Would you just follow along as I read in English. I'm going to start at the top of the B/C/S page; and on the English page, it will be the second chunk of text underneath paragraph 5. "Prepare the takeover of staff, buildings, and equipment of Security Service Centres and their integration with the newly established organ of the interior at the seat of the centre." First question: Did I read that accurately?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Moving on, I understand that you say you have not seen this document before; but in your time as a political leader in Srpsko Novo Sarajevo, were in fact Security Service Centres taken over by the Serbian or the Republika Srpska government in order that they could be merged into a new Security Service Centre?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the outbreak of the conflict? Are you asking me about the period before the outbreak of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm leaving the time open ended, and I'm asking you if, in fact, as this document indicates, the government of Srpsko Sarajevo, in fact, took over and merged the Security Service Centres, as describes in the chunk of text I just read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic has a point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness should really know what time-frame we are talking about. What's the date of this document? We always so far showed the witness the time that is relevant and the date, and that applied equally to the Prosecution and the Defence. Can we please be told which period we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President, before the break, the cover page was shown to the witness and it has a date of October 1991 -- excuse me, 19th of December, 1991. May the witness answer the question, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know anything about this and whether this organisation was set up. However, after reading the document during the break in its entirety, I've seen that when, in 2004, I was interviewed by the investigator and shown this same document, but I don't know whether anything was done or carried out with regard to this particular paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Let me ask -- let me ask you this: During your evidence in-chief, you testified that when you were the president of the assembly, you were briefed by the MUP chief for east Sarajevo every morning. Do you recall giving that evidence, and was that correct evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In wartime conditions, we had regular early mornings to hear about the situation in Novo Sarajevo municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. Now, during those early mornings briefings, since they happened every day, I take it you got to know the MUP chief reasonably well. Fair assumption on my part?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And did the MUP chief work for a merged security centre as described in paragraph 5, or did he continue to work for the old Security Services Centre, the old pre-war institution, before the partition of the city?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He worked for the Security Services Centre of Republika Srpska after 1993 when I was the president of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Give us an idea, if you could, Mr. Katic, give some examples of topics that would be covered at this morning briefing with the MUP chief.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first topic would be whether there had been any incidents in Grbavica. When I say "incidents," that means if there were any assaults amongst civilians; whether anyone broke in -- into the Mis building where humanitarian aid was being distributed; and whether everything with regard to everyday life was functioning properly; whether there were in the burglaries, any burglarised flats, and information to that effect. So we were solely focussed on civilian affairs that affected the life of citizens in Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. And the reason I have been asking these questions about the MUP is because during area evidence in-chief, you testified about criminal activity in Grbavica, do you remember that, and in particular, about criminal gangs operating in Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Do you also recall in August of last year, when you met with Mr. Hogan and Mr. Sachdeva, indicating that those criminal gangs were brought under control by the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And, in fact, those criminal gangs were either brought into the command structure, the chain of command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, or they were broken up forcibly by law enforcement; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Broken up forcibly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He never said, and I would kindly ask the Prosecutor just as I had been warned on occasions to indicate exactly when these witness said that these gangs were involved in the activities of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. He did mention certain things, but never said that for the record, that there were gangs involved in the activities of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. If that is the case, I would like the Prosecutor to indicate exactly in the transcript of this proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty, since you're being challenged, refer us to the pages and the witness statement of the -- this is a statement taken by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: This is a statement taken in August of 2006. It was reduced to an information report, and Mr. Tapuskovic has misunderstood. I'm not saying that there were criminal gangs involved in the operation of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. I am saying that the opposite. I am saying that they were not involved. I am rebutting a claim that there were rogue elements operating in Grbavica. So I can't respond to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did follow that, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really cannot check the English version. I understand in B/C/S that it was said twice that those gangs were involved in the activities of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. If Mr. Docherty insists that this is not what was said, then I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: So what I'm saying, Mr. Katic, is that these gangs were brought under control by the MUP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who were not gangs of large proportions. Those were individuals. We specifically had problems with a couple of people who had killed the president of the executive committee on the 25th of April, 1994. They also killed a company commander. That is when MUP got involved, arrested the first man who killed the president of the executive committee in his office at his workplace; and during the arrest of the second person who did not want to surrender, members of the MUP shot him dead. There were such individuals. But with more stringent measures applied by the MUP, this ebbed away. There were no incidents involving seizure of humanitarian aid from the premises where it was being distributed, nor assaults on civilians irrespective of their ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: So the -- going on from that, you also testified in your evidence in-chief and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, this is transcript 6031, lines 10 through 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You also testified that from time to time utilities, specifically electricity, needed to be repaired, and that repairmen from both sides, together with UNPROFOR, would make sure that there were joint interventions in order that no one got hurt during the repair of the electricity lines. Do you remember that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And so that would involve, would it not, arranging a temporary cease-fire in order that this electrical repair work could be done without risk to the repair personnel; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. But, particularly, in 1994, there was almost constant cease-fire in Grbavica, in cooperation. When representatives of UNPROFOR and the electric company on both sides and also with representatives of the gas or water works companies, it was agreed to have this repair work done by jointly formed work details, and this practice was pursued in 1994 and 1994, all the way up to the time of the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. But this would also require - correct me if I'm wrong - would also require that the shooting stop in order that these joint work details don't get hurt; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the final security measure that had to be taken pursuant to these agreements.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And it was possible for the barracks -- for the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command to issue orders that this fire stop in order that the joint work detail could carry out its job, and these orders would be implemented; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Last question regarding the police or the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And if we could see please 65 ter number -- first, could we tender the document that is on the screen, and then have I another document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P757, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And the next document is 65 ter number 03187. We'll take a look at the cover page, and then move to paragraph number 6. And, Your Honour, this is the document which Mr. Tapuskovic had an objection at the close of the day on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Katic, on the screen in front of you is a document from the Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality of Novo Sarajevo. It's dated November the -- I am sorry, 5th of June of 1992. And I know have you testified that you were not a member of the Crisis Staff, but you have also testified about some level of familiarity with the MUP and with the police, and that is what I want to ask you about in this document. First of all, does it appear to be an authentic document from the Crisis Staff of Srpsko Novo Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Could we now look at paragraph numbered 6 in both the English and the B/C/S versions, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Under paragraph 6, there are three blocks of text. I'm really only interested in the top one: "Citizens of all nationalities assemble frequently, especially in Grbavica, and our public attitude is very correct. We appoint a head of every building who is responsible for the situation in his building and for all the information about the occupants. Secretly, the police apply the usual procedure to people who were engaged in military activities against us." My first question, Mr. Katic, is whether I read that correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: In your meetings with the MUP chief every morning, while you were president of the assembly, did he enlighten you as to what is meant by "the usual procedures"?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The MUP chief, during the time when I was the president, knew nothing about it, just like I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: So you don't know what these "usual procedures" are that are applied in secret, even though "our public attitude is very correct"?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I see here was written by the Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality of Novo Sarajevo. I wasn't a member of either the municipal committee or the Crisis Staff of Novo Sarajevo municipality; therefore, I don't know details about this. I never went there or took part in the Crisis Staff meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I understand that you were never a member of the Crisis Staff and I understand you did not go to Crisis Staff meetings, but you have testified to quite a level of familiarity with the MUP, and that is why I asked you the question. But you do not know what the usual methods are?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ne. [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I have one other document I would like to show you with concern of the treatment of civilians in the Grbavica area?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And so, once again, Mr. President, can I tender the document that is on the screen, and then I will have another document to call up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P758, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And the last document is actually a Defence exhibit. It was put into evidence. The document identification number was DD00-3213.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Do you remember this document, Mr. Katic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, this was presented during your evidence in-chief, and it was about the shooting of a woman who was apparently trying to cross the lines. I have a few questions about this document. It's in evidence, by the way, as Defence Exhibit 205. First of all, the event that's being described happened on the 6th of April, didn't it? And this document is dated the 7th of April, and it talks about "last night." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just see. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: It occurred at 7.30 in the evening, because it says: "Last night around 1930," which in military time is 7.30 in the evening; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: In Sarajevo on the 6th of April, it's dark at 7.30 in the evening, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And we have here a report not from the army of Republika Srpska or any Serbian organ, but, rather, from the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina command; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. Of the shooting of a person who was wandering around a combat -- moving around, I should say, in a combat area during the dark, in fact, in the no man's land between two opposing arms. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just read everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see no man's land mentioned anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: It's not in the document. That is my characterisation of the document.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I thought you were reading out from the document, and I can't find "no man's land" anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. Ready to go on?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: So this is a shooting, accidental and tragic, but of a person who was in the dark near two opposing armies; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it says here she wanted to cross to the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Okay. But it was in the dark; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's as dark probably as it is here at 10.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And it's in the area between -- in the neighbourhood of a couple of opposing armies; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And a report has been made of the incident by the army whose soldier shot the person; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And that report doesn't say that this was faked by the Serbian side or that this was part of a propaganda ploy to besmirch the army of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army, does it; rather, it just sets out that this happened. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I have no further questions about that document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And at what stage will have you no further questionings at all, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to hear you're anticipating that, Your Honour. I have one more topic to cover with Mr. Katic, and I think I will finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Then proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Katic, the last area I want to talk with you about is during your examination-in-chief, you talked about the total exclusion zone; and, in fact, you have mentioned it earlier when -- in your cross-examination when we were talking about the tank in Grbavica. Do you remember these bits of testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: The total exclusion zone or heavy weapons exclusion zone, that was put into place following the first bombing of the Markale market in February of 1994; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm just going to run through what this weapons exclusion zone meant in practice. Under this agreement, heavy weapons had to be either taken at least 20 kilometres out of the town, or put into a Weapon Collection Points, or guarded by UNPROFOR troops. Is my understanding of the terms of this agreement the same as your understanding?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And I just want to run through some of the things that UNPROFOR was doing at this time besides guarding weapons or Weapon Collection Points. UNPROFOR had responsibility for seeing to it that humanitarian aid convoys got into the city or got to the people who needed the humanitarian aid. Do you agree that that is one of UNPROFOR's tasks at this point?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: By February of 1994, UNPROFOR was also operating the Sarajevo airport; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: As you mentioned, or as you testified to a few moments ago, UNPROFOR was assisting in the restoration of utilities and other public services; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Would you agree that UNPROFOR was also trying to identify as accurately and as quickly as possible cease-fire violations and protect the civilian population as much as possible from the ravages of war?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Would you agree that as a result of all these tasks that UNPROFOR had to perform, security over these Weapon Collection Points or over weapons that were under guard was often not adequate and that those weapons could be and were fired at the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I will say the following: The weapons that had been removed and stored in area of responsibility to the south of Sarajevo, in Tvrdimici and Petrovici, that's not 20 kilometres as the crow flies. But in agreement with the corps, UNPROFOR, and liaison officers, those weapons were stored at those sites. It was covered with netting, with branches; and 24 hours a day, those points were guarded by UNPROFOR and the Republika Srpska army troops. And I can confirm that because I accompanied UNPROFOR members to Tvrdimici and to Petrovici to verify, so that we in the civilian authorities could verify what the situation was with those weapons. As for the other areas around Sarajevo where heavy weapons had been removed to and stored, I cannot give you any specific anticipates because I did not go to those sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Well, in any event, Mr. Katic, when you went out and saw the weapons covered with netting and branches, was that shortly after the agreement was entered into in February of 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as the February 1994 agreement was reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I want to talk to you, Mr. Katic, about some things that happened after the agreement was reached and during the dime that Dragomir Milosevic had taken over command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps; that is to say, after August of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: To begin with, could we see 65 ter number 01984, and this is already in evidence as Prosecution Exhibit 667. And could we go to the second page of the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: This is an order, Mr. Katic, from General Milosevic, and I particularly draw your attention to paragraph 3, under the word "Order." "Order that all heavy weapons in the 20 kilometre zone around Sarajevo be camouflaged and hidden in solid buildings, move heavy weapons through the 20 kilometre zone only in accordance with the orders of the corps commander during the night." Do you see that, Mr. Katic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And we could go back to the first page, if you want to. This is dated the 21st of August, 1994. Do you accept that or do you want to see the first page with the date? Or scroll to the top of the --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I can see that, so I accept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, following this, Mr. Katic, are you aware, just to take a few examples, of a modified air bomb launched on Hrasnica on 7th of April, 1995? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. Are you aware of a modified air bomb launched against the Bosnia-Herzegovina TV tower on the 28th of June, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Earlier today I showed you a document in evidence as Prosecution Exhibit 33, that was the letter from General Gobillard to General Milosevic complaining about an artillery attack all along the line. When I showed it to you, I was concentrating on the line about the tank in Grbavica, but do you recall that Prosecution Exhibit 33 also talked about artillery all along the line being used?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the document. I saw that earlier on in my evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And so you are aware that after -- after February of 1994 and after this order to camouflage heavy weapons, but keep them in the 20-kilometre exclusion zone, artillery and modified air bombs continued to be used?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I don't know about that. I've already said that I had no idea what kind of bombs we're talking about, modified bombs. Although, I had worked at Pretis, I had never seen that, and this is what I stated to the investigators last year in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 33, though, talks about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, I have a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were talking of the exclusion zone, in which no weapons should be used, and you are saying that these modified bombs were being sent out, but you were also saying that heavy weapons were being used. I do not feel that both these elements come from the same document, or are they coming from the same document, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You are right, Judge Mindua. They are coming from separate documents: The one about camouflages weapons, which is on the screen, and then Prosecution Exhibit 33, which we talked about with the witness earlier. I'm not showing it, again, just because we have seen it a couple of times. I can if it would be helpful, but I just thought I would ask him one or two brief questions about that document. So I am putting this document on the screen, the camouflage document, and then asking the witness about various uses of heavy weapons, whether it is Hrasnica, the TV tower, the June protest letter from General Gobillard, what have you. All dealing with heavy weapons being used in Sarajevo. Is that responsive to your question, Judge Mindua?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I think it's clear now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Are you familiar, Mr. Katic, with an attack on the Bosnia-Herzegovina Presidency on the 2nd of December, 1994, which investigation established was done with wire-guided missiles. Are you familiar with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: If we could please see Prosecution Exhibit 329, please, and, I'm sorry -- if we could see the second page, please. I believe there should be an English translation, at least I've read it. I'm just asking if the corresponding -- the B/C/S page corresponding to the English page that's on the left could be displayed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the two pages -- okay. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Do you see here that this is another protest letter from General Gobillard to General Milosevic and that one of the things that he is complaining about is the launching of four missiles, including the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Do you understand that it is relative straightforward to figure out where a wire-guided missile was launched from because, really, all you have to do is walk back along the wire until you come to the launching point?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, all those things that you showed to me, all those documents, are of military nature; and in my evidence, I've explained that I held only civilian posts. And all my dealings with the military were of a humanitarian nature, and here you see four projectiles had been fired and only three targets had been hit. So, immediately, you can see that the first part and the latter part, it doesn't really tally. I don't know what is actually meant by AT-12, AT-3. I really don't know what kind of weapons we're talking about, so I can't tell you where all this had been fired from and where it had been launched from.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Katic, I understand that you were not, at the time of this letter, in the armed forces. But with all respect, sir, on your direct examination, when you were asked things like the location of the confrontation lines around Debelo Brdo, you did not then object that this called for military knowledge and that you were a civilian, did you? To take one example among many I could cite.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, but I don't know anything about those weapons. I spoke about what I knew, infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Katic, Mr. Martin Bell, a British BBC correspondent, testified in this trial concerning the incident that is the subject of this letter; and, in fact, there is a film of this, and I'm going show that film to you now and ask whether what you observe is perhaps the result of a heavy weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Ms. Bosnjakovic, can we please play Prosecution Exhibit 620.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: We can stop now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: That wasn't an infantry --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: That wasn't an infantry weapon, was it, Mr. Katic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And that building, it is the Presidency, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the building of Presidency, but I don't know what exploded in front of that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Whatever it was, though, it was not an infantry weapon, a light infantry weapon?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was not an infantry weapon, but I don't know what exploded there in front of that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Doesn't the letter from General Gobillard tell you what exploded, not in front of the building, but on the building?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With all due respect to Mr. Gobillard, when I see this footage, all I can say is that was not caused by an infantry weapon. But as to what it really was, I cannot tell you. Whether this was this AT-3 weapon, I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And I understand that, and I'm not asking you for that. Mr. Katic, that order that we saw from General Milosevic to hide the heavy weapons, to camouflage them, to move them at night, I put it to you that General Milosevic is ordering those heavy weapons to be hidden in violation of the heavy weapon exclusion zone, so as to have ready to hand the means needed to continue a campaign of terror against the civilians of Sarajevo by deliberately them for sniping and for shelling. Do you agree or disagree with the proposition I've just put to you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let me hear Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document that has been discussed now does not mention snipers anywhere. The document that the witness saw, the sniper could not have been camouflaged. This is something that does not exist in the document and, again, we have hypothesis. This is not contained in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I don't really understand that objection. I put it to the witness that the weapons were being hidden in order to continue a campaign, and that campaign had to components: Deliberate targeting by shelling, deliberate targeting by sniping. And I asked if this order was in furtherance to that campaign, and I don't think there is anything objectionable with document, even though it talks about heavy weapons being in furtherance of a campaign that more generally includes other means of terror.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty, I think it is perfectly proper to put the witness that General Milosevic orders those heavy weapons to be hidden, but the purpose of that order I don't consider to be a proper matter for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: For the record, I am putting my case to the witness as required by Rule 90(H) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. However, with that noted for the record, I will certainly rephrase the question as Your Honour suggests.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Katic, in that order, General Milosevic is not directing that those weapons be moved 20 kilometres out of town, is he?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in accordance with the order, the heavy weapons had to be removed at a distance of 20 kilometres from the city. And I have already said that in the Novo Sarajevo municipality, in Petrovici and Tvrdimici site, this is was where it was done, and it was guarded 24 hours a day by UNPROFOR and Republika Srpska army soldiers. Only the three or four armoured personnel cars had not been removed from Grbavica, but they were positioned behind the buildings in the doorways all the time, and they controlled by UNPROFOR. And let me tell you this. If those weapons, despite the 24-hour a day control by UNPROFOR, was used, then those UNPROFOR members who were supposed to guard them had to be held responsible. I can only talk about the areas that I myself saw. I cannot say anything about the areas to the north of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Katic, I'm going to ask the question, again, and I'll ask you to please answer the question put to you. The document that you saw from General Milosevic ordering the weapons to be camouflaged and hidden and moved only at night, I'm asking about that document, that document does not say: Move the weapons 20 kilometres out of town, does it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But it does order for the weapons to be concealed and to work day and night to remove the weapons. Because if you can not do that in three days, then you had to work around the clock to remove those weapons. Because if the agreement stipulated that had you to do it within five or ten days, and if you were unable to do that by working solely by day, you had to work through the night to do it, to group the weapons where they were supposed to be put, and not as you are putting to me, to store them by day and then use them by night. That is not something that I can accept.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Katic, that document doesn't have the verb "to remove" anywhere in it, does it? We can call it back up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you please call it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let it be displayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: 65 ter number 01984.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And my question, Mr. Katic, is this document talks about concealing and hiding weapons, doesn't it? It doesn't say remove them from the 20-kilometre exclusion zone. It says, "hide them." And I put it to you, and this is my question, that is the only fair reading of this document?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under item 3, it says: "Order, the camouflage and hiding in solid facilities, garage, basements of all heavy weapon in the 20-kilometre zone around Sarajevo; Move heavy weapons through the 20-kilometre zone only in accordance with the orders of the corps commander, during the night; and take all police and other security measures so that if need arises for such movements, they will be concealed from UNPROFOR forces."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So what it says here is --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Do you wish to conclude your sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says here: "Order that all heavy weapons in the 20-kilometre zone around Sarajevo be camouflaged and hidden in solid buildings." That's what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, we are at the time when we have to break for the day, so regrettably you will have to come back tomorrow if Mr. Tapuskovic wishes to re-examine. So I ask, Mr. Tapuskovic: Do you wish to re-examine?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I do have a number of questions that I really have to ask of this witness. I thought I would be willing to release him, but I do have some questions that I have to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. We are adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 5th day of June, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
